transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you lately or what brings you in today?

I guess the main thing is… at work, on the floor, I keep losing my train of thought. I’m a nurse, and I try really hard to stay on top of everything, but if an IV pump starts beeping, or someone asks another nurse a question near me, or a call light goes off, I suddenly realize I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on.

It’s probably not as dramatic as it sounds, but it’s been happening enough that I thought I should come in and talk to someone about it.
Do you often find it hard to focus or stay attentive, especially in situations with a lot of distractions or activity?

Yes… I think that’s really the main thing. I don’t want to make it sound like I can’t do my job, because I do try really hard, but on the floor, with everything going on, I lose my train of thought constantly.

Like an IV pump beeps, or someone nearby asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’m just… blank for a second. I’ll realize I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was in the middle of working on. It’s embarrassing to admit, but yes, distractions really throw me off.
Do you experience these lapses in focus only at work, or do they also happen in quieter, less distracting environments like at home or during conversations?

It’s mostly at work, I think… or at least that’s where I notice it the most, because the floor is so busy and there are so many things pulling at my attention.

I don’t want to overstate it, but the main reason I came in is that I lose my train of thought there constantly. Like, I’ll be working through a patient flow issue, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone nearby asks another nurse something, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’m just… I’ve completely dropped what I was doing.

I guess I notice it most when there are distractions around me, if that makes sense.

When you're at home, or in a quiet setting like watching TV or reading, do you still find yourself losing focus or forgetting what you were doing, or does this mainly happen when you're on the busy hospital floor?

It mainly happens on the hospital floor, or at least that’s where it feels really obvious. I’m not saying I never drift at home, but the thing that’s been worrying me is work.

Like I’ll be trying to sort out a patient flow issue, and then an IV pump beeps or a call light goes off, or someone nearby asks another nurse a question, and I just… lose the whole thread. Then I’m standing there trying to remember what I was just doing. It feels silly to say, but that’s the part that made me think I should ask someone about it.
When you're at home doing something quiet, like watching TV or reading, do you ever lose your train of thought the same way you described happening at work?

At home it’s… not really the same, I don’t think. I mean, I can zone out a little like anyone, but the thing that feels like a problem is really on the floor.

That’s why I’m here, honestly. I’ll be in the middle of figuring out a patient flow issue, and then an IV pump beeps or a call light goes off, or someone nearby asks another nurse something, and suddenly I’ve just lost the thread completely. Then I’m standing there trying to remember what I was doing. I don’t know if that makes sense, but that’s the part that’s been bothering me.

When you're doing something that requires your attention at home, like following a conversation, cooking, or managing tasks, do you ever find yourself losing focus or forgetting what you were doing, even without distractions around you?

I mean… without distractions, I’m not sure it happens in the same way. At home I can usually get by, I think.

The main thing — and I know I’ve said this already — is really on the floor. I’ll be in the middle of working through some patient flow issue, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone asks another nurse something, or a call light goes off, and it’s like the thought just disappears. I suddenly can’t remember what I was doing or what step I was on.

So I guess I notice it most when something pulls my attention away. That’s the part that feels constant and embarrassing, honestly.

Have you had trouble with focus or losing your train of thought in less stimulating environments, like at home, for most of your life, or is this something that only started recently or only happens under stress at work?

I guess… if I’m being honest, it’s not completely new. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was, because I did fine in school overall, but even in elementary school my teachers would write things like I was bright but careless.

I was always losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework, and my mom had to sit with me every night to keep me on track. I kind of wrote that off as just being a kid, but maybe it’s relevant?
Looking back, did you have similar issues with losing your train of thought, getting distracted, or forgetting tasks when you were a child, even outside of school?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t remember every detail outside of school, but even in elementary school there were signs, I guess.

My teachers would say I was bright but careless, which always felt a little embarrassing. I was the kid losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework even when I’d done it. And my mom pretty much had to sit with me every night to keep me moving and make sure I stayed on track.

I didn’t think of it as a big problem at the time, but looking back… yeah, it was there.

Besides work and when you were in school, do you find yourself losing focus or getting distracted easily in other parts of your life now, like when you’re running errands, driving, or having a conversation?

I guess in other parts of life it happens some, but… honestly, the clearest and most embarrassing place is still work.

Like I’ll be on the floor trying to sort through a patient flow issue, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly the whole thread is just gone. I’ll be standing there thinking, wait, what was I doing? What step was I on?

So I don’t want to overstate it with errands or driving if I’m not totally sure, but that losing-my-train-of-thought thing is definitely happening there. Does that answer what you mean?
Outside of work and when you were in school, do you often find yourself losing focus or getting distracted during everyday activities like running errands, having a conversation, or driving?

I mean… I notice it a little in daily life, but I don’t want to exaggerate if I’m not sure.

The main reason I’m here is really what happens on the floor. I’ll be trying to work through a patient flow issue, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone asks another nurse something, or a call light goes off, and it’s like the whole thought just disappears. I’ll have to stop and think, “Wait, what was I doing?” or “What step was I on?”

So, outside of work I guess maybe sometimes, but the constant, really disruptive version is at work. Is that still helpful to answer it that way?
Looking back, did you have difficulty organizing tasks or activities during childhood, even outside of school, such as keeping your room tidy or finishing chores at home?

I’m not totally sure how much I remember from childhood with that specifically… I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was.

But organizing things has definitely always felt harder for me than it seems like it should. Even now, when I’m charge nurse, I’ll have scraps of paper and sticky notes and these half-started lists everywhere, like I’m trying to be organized, but I still can’t always figure out what needs to happen first. So I end up just handling whatever problem is loudest in the moment, and then I’m rushing at the end of the shift to catch up.

So… I guess if that counts as the same kind of thing, then yes, it does fit.
Do you find it hard to organize your daily activities or stay focused on tasks outside of work, such as managing your schedule, completing household tasks, or staying on track during a conversation?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m incapable of managing things, because I do get through the day, but organizing the order of things is hard for me.

Like when I’m charge nurse, I’ll have scraps of paper, sticky notes, half-started lists all over, and I’m trying to keep track of everything. But I still can’t always decide what needs to happen first. So I end up just dealing with whatever feels most urgent or whatever is loudest right then, and then by the end of the shift I’m rushing to catch up.

So yes, I think organizing and staying on track is a problem for me… if that’s what you mean.
Have you ever had trouble finishing projects with friends or family, or found that others are frustrated with you because you lose focus or forget things during social plans or shared tasks?

Yeah… I think that happens. I feel bad saying it because I’m not trying to be careless or unreliable.

It’s more like I’ll fully intend to do something, like call a family member back, pay a bill, or show up for an appointment, and then somehow it just drops out of my head. Sometimes I even set a reminder, and I still manage to miss it or swipe it away and forget again.

At work it can be things like meaning to follow up on a missing order, and then getting pulled into something else and realizing later I never circled back. I know that can frustrate people, and honestly it frustrates me too. I don’t want people to think I don’t care, because I do.
Looking back, would you say these issues with focus and getting distracted were definitely present before you turned 12, or did they start more recently, especially related to work stress?

I think they were there before 12, yes… at least from what I can remember and what my mom has told me.

I did well enough that I don’t think it looked like a huge problem, but even in elementary school my teachers would write things like I was bright but careless. I was always losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework. And my mom pretty much had to sit with me every night to keep me on track, otherwise I’d drift off or not finish.

So… I don’t think it’s just work stress now. Work probably makes it more obvious, but it was there when I was little too.

I mean… I notice it a little in daily life, but I don’t want to exaggerate if I’m not sure.

The main reason I’m here is really what happens on the floor. I’ll be trying to work through a patient flow issue, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone asks another nurse something, or a call light goes off, and it’s like the whole thought just disappears. I’ll have to stop and think, “Wait, what was I doing?” or “What step was I on?”

So, outside of work I guess maybe sometimes, but the constant, really disruptive version is at work. Is that still helpful to answer it that way?

doctor.question: Looking back, did you have difficulty organizing tasks or activities during childhood, even outside of school, such as keeping your room tidy or finishing chores at home?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When I’m charge nurse, I have scraps of paper, sticky notes, and half-started lists everywhere, but I still can’t seem to decide what has to happen first, so I end up putting out whatever fire is loudest and then rushing at the end of the shift.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about difficulty organizing tasks or activities, including chores and keeping things tidy in childhood.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how much I remember from childhood with that specifically… I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was.

But organizing things has definitely always felt harder for me than it seems like it should. Even now, when I’m charge nurse, I’ll have scraps of paper and sticky notes and these half-started lists everywhere, like I’m trying to be organized, but I still can’t always figure out what needs to happen first. So I end up just handling whatever problem is loudest in the moment, and then I’m rushing at the end of the shift to catch up.

So… I guess if that counts as the same kind of thing, then yes, it does fit.

doctor.question: Do you find it hard to organize your daily activities or stay focused on tasks outside of work, such as managing your schedule, completing household tasks, or staying on track during a conversation?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When I’m charge nurse, I have scraps of paper, sticky notes, and half-started lists everywhere, but I still can’t seem to decide what has to happen first, so I end up putting out whatever fire is loudest and then rushing at the end of the shift.
target_item.reason: The question is mainly asking about difficulty organizing daily activities and managing tasks outside of work, such as schedules and household tasks.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m incapable of managing things, because I do get through the day, but organizing the order of things is hard for me.

Like when I’m charge nurse, I’ll have scraps of paper, sticky notes, half-started lists all over, and I’m trying to keep track of everything. But I still can’t always decide what needs to happen first. So I end up just dealing with whatever feels most urgent or whatever is loudest right then, and then by the end of the shift I’m rushing to catch up.

So yes, I think organizing and staying on track is a problem for me… if that’s what you mean.

inference.note: The patient's lifelong pattern of inattention, distractibility, and difficulties with organization both in childhood and currently across multiple settings (work, home, school) supports ADHD (F90.0). The presence of stress-related focus difficulties could also support an adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.10). However, the patient’s persistent, lifelong symptoms make F54 (nondependent personality traits) less likely, as these are not primarily associated with the cognitive symptoms described.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient meets criteria for functional impairment in social or occupational domains beyond the workplace, which is relevant to the diagnosis of ADHD (F90.0) versus Adjustment Disorder (F43.10).
doctor.question: Have you ever had trouble finishing projects with friends or family, or found that others are frustrated with you because you lose focus or forget things during social plans or shared tasks?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: I forget things that should be routine, like calling a family member back, following up on a missing order, paying a bill at home, or showing up for an appointment, even when I meant to do it and sometimes even after I set a reminder.
target_item.reason: The question asks about forgetting things or losing focus during social plans and shared tasks, especially others being frustrated due to forgetfulness in daily activities.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think that happens. I feel bad saying it because I’m not trying to be careless or unreliable.

It’s more like I’ll fully intend to do something, like call a family member back, pay a bill, or show up for an appointment, and then somehow it just drops out of my head. Sometimes I even set a reminder, and I still manage to miss it or swipe it away and forget again.

At work it can be things like meaning to follow up on a missing order, and then getting pulled into something else and realizing later I never circled back. I know that can frustrate people, and honestly it frustrates me too. I don’t want people to think I don’t care, because I do.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient meets the symptom duration criteria for ADHD (i.e., symptoms present before age 12) versus whether these difficulties might be better explained by an adjustment reaction or situational stress at work.
doctor.question: Looking back, would you say these issues with focus and getting distracted were definitely present before you turned 12, or did they start more recently, especially related to work stress?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, my teachers wrote that I was bright but careless and always losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework, and my mom had to sit with me every night to keep me on track.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the focus and distractibility issues were present before age 12 versus starting more recently.

patient.answer:
I think they were there before 12, yes… at least from what I can remember and what my mom has told me.

I did well enough that I don’t think it looked like a huge problem, but even in elementary school my teachers would write things like I was bright but careless. I was always losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework. And my mom pretty much had to sit with me every night to keep me on track, otherwise I’d drift off or not finish.

So… I don’t think it’s just work stress now. Work probably makes it more obvious, but it was there when I was little too.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of inattention, distractibility, and difficulties with organization and task completion have been present since childhood, predating the work stress. This supports a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. The chronic nature of the symptoms and their presence in multiple settings (school, home, and work) rule out other disorders such as adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct or attentional issues due to stress alone. The symptoms are not better explained by an anxiety or mood disorder, and there is no evidence of hyperactivity or impulsivity that would support a combined presentation.
